name: Victor Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the assistant stockman at Long Meadow, a beef farm with about a hundred and eighty suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves, plus the bulls and youngstock. In winter they're all in the sheds, so my day starts at half six with feeding: silage in the feed passage, straw for bedding, checking for anyone off their food or lame. In summer it's grass and hay, and the hay is half the business, because Mrs Okafor sells small bales to horse owners all over the county.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle. You get to know them, which one will push the gate, which one is a good mother. What wears me out is hay time, because it's all about the weather and you're baling until midnight if the rain's coming. And the paperwork for cattle passports, every calf has to be registered within days or you're in trouble.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, she took it on when her husband died eight years ago. She's sharp, she does the numbers, I do the muck. I've been there three years, came from a job at a builders' merchant. I'm still not great with calving, I panic a bit when it goes wrong, but I'm getting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool. I'd tell people I already ask it about the weather sometimes. Nobody at the cattle market would care much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of help with the calf registrations would be nice. I use one of those AI chats now and then, mostly to write the hay adverts for Facebook, because I'm not good with words. If it's better, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Keep learning calving from Mrs Okafor and the vet. Me and Kira have about two months saved, maybe a bit more, and I'd just keep adding to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the hay advert usually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small bales, good meadow hay, dust-free, collection or delivery, and the price. The AI made it sound a lot posher than that, something about sunshine and wildflowers. Sold more bales though, so maybe it knew something I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Kira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner. She works in the bakery at the big supermarket in town, early starts like me, so we're both asleep by nine. We've been together four years and we rent a little house on Brook Lane.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, and I already ask it about the weather sometimes. Nobody at the cattle market would care much.
S0.think: A bit of help with calf registrations would be nice. I use AI chat now and then to write hay adverts because I'm not good with words, so if it gets better, fine.
S0.do: Keeps learning calving from Mrs Okafor and the vet. Adds steadily to the two months or so of savings he shares with his partner Kira.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: The AI made it sound a lot posher than that, something about sunshine and wildflowers. Sold more bales though, so maybe it knew something I didn't.
S0.fieldNote: Victor uses AI casually and is amused by it rather than impressed. His real learning curve is calving, which makes him nervous. A practical, easy-going start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine, gives everyone time. If firms hire fewer beginners, that's bad for young people trying to get in, and somebody should look at apprenticeships. But I wouldn't make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm probably all right. Cattle need hands. The bit I'd think about is Mrs Okafor, she's in her late fifties, and if she slows down, will she get a manager or a computer to do her side?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her to start showing me the money side, the cattle sales, what a calf costs to rear. If I knew more of that, I'd be worth more. Maybe a short course at the college on farm business, if it's a few evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little uneasy about the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a calf cost to rear, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly, and that's the point. I know what they eat and how much straw goes down, but I couldn't tell you if we make money on a calf. Mrs Okafor keeps that in her head and on a laptop I've never touched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody should look at apprenticeships. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The colleges and the farm groups, with a bit of help from government, probably. It's not one side's job. My cousin did a proper apprenticeship as an electrician and he's doing better than any of us.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is fine and gives everyone time. Fewer jobs for beginners is bad, and somebody should look at apprenticeships, but I wouldn't make a big thing of it.
S1.think: I think I'm probably fine, because cattle need hands. What I'd wonder about is Mrs Okafor's side of the business, and whether a manager or a computer would take it over as she slows down.
S1.do: Asks Mrs Okafor to teach him the money side of the herd, like sales and rearing costs. Signs up for a few evenings of a farm business course at the college.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, a little uneasy about the long run.
S1.quote: I know what they eat and how much straw goes down, but I couldn't tell you if we make money on a calf.
S1.fieldNote: He spotted his own blind spot without being pushed: he doesn't know the farm's numbers. His instinct is to fill the gap step by step. He's calm, but thinking ahead more than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rough for office people, and both parties should stop shouting and actually agree something. I don't think it's one side's fault. I'd say that at the market, and I'd probably not bother online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's the thing I'd really think. Our hay buyers are horse owners, and a lot of them work in offices in town. If they lose jobs or take pay cuts, the pony is the first thing to go, and so do our hay sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mrs Okafor early, before summer, that we might sell less hay to horse people. We could look at selling more to other farms, or making more silage for our own cattle instead. And Kira and I would hold off on the holiday we were planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my job, for the farm's money, which ends up being my job anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did that happen before, horse owners cutting back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor says yes, years ago, when money was tight everywhere. She said people were giving ponies away for free, and the hay sat in the barn till spring. She remembers it because the barn roof leaked that year too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some new AI jobs appear in this picture. Would you look at any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it was near home and to do with farms, like the software for cattle records. I'd want to hear from someone who'd done it for a year first. I'm not jumping into something because it's new.

S2.say: I'd say it's rough for office workers and both parties should stop shouting and agree something. I'd say it at the market but wouldn't bother online.
S2.think: Our hay buyers are mostly horse owners with office jobs in town. If they lose work, the pony goes first, and so do our hay sales.
S2.do: Warns Mrs Okafor before summer that hay sales to horse owners may fall, and suggests selling to other farms or making more silage. Postpones the holiday he and Kira had planned.
S2.feel: Uneasy for the farm's income, which he knows is his job in the end.
S2.quote: If they lose jobs or take pay cuts, the pony is the first thing to go, and so do our hay sales.
S2.fieldNote: He made a link I hadn't expected: office layoffs reach the farm through the horse owners who buy hay. He thinks about the business like an owner, even though he's junior. He refuses to blame one side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if some people are getting rich on shares while others lose everything, that needs fixing, but sensibly. Tax it a bit, help people retrain. I'd say that to anyone who asked, but I'm not marching anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's mixed for us. The rich ones with shares keep their horses and might buy more, so hay might hold up. But if Kira's bakery job went, or our rent went up with house prices, I'd feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Mrs Okafor to sell hay to the better-off buyers, the livery yards and the people with land. I'd ask about living in the farm's old caravan, just to save the rent for a year, though Kira would need convincing. And I'd keep the savings for emergencies only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like you're safe at work but the ground around you is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Kira live in a caravan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. She'd say for a month, maybe. It's got a wood stove and a leaky window. I'd have to fix the window first or there's no deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you blame anyone in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really one person. It'd be the AI companies doing well and the government being slow, same as always. Blaming doesn't feed the cows, though.

S3.say: I'd say if some people get rich on shares while others lose everything, it needs fixing sensibly, with some tax and help to retrain. I'd say that to anyone, but I wouldn't march.
S3.think: It's mixed for us: rich horse owners might keep buying hay. But if Kira's bakery job went or house prices pushed our rent up, I'd feel it straight away.
S3.do: Pushes Mrs Okafor to sell hay to livery yards and wealthier buyers. Proposes living in the farm's old caravan for a year to save on rent, after fixing its leaky window.
S3.feel: Anxious, safe at work but with the ground moving around him.
S3.quote: Ha. She'd say for a month, maybe. It's got a wood stove and a leaky window. I'd have to fix the window first or there's no deal.
S3.fieldNote: He's still calculating the business angle, aiming hay at better-off buyers. The caravan plan shows he'd make real sacrifices to protect savings. Funny, but the worry about rent and Kira's job was there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for farm workers this time, and the robot makers should pay into it. Not angry, just fair. If they want robots on farms, fine, but people need somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a robot feeder already exists, it drives up the feed passage and pushes the silage on its own. A farm down the road has one. If Mrs Okafor bought one, and a robot for the bedding, half my morning is gone, and I'm the junior, so I'm the half that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see if the neighbour's feeder actually works through a whole winter, then I'd ask to be the one trained on it. I'd save harder, maybe four hundred a month instead of two. And I'd quietly look at jobs with the vet practice or the cattle market, places that need people who can handle cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the sums look like at three in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, car, Kira's wage, mine at maybe half. We'd last about four months, then it's back to my mum's spare room. I'd hate telling her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see if the feeder works. Is waiting safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, you're right. If I wait a whole winter, someone else might be the one trained. Maybe I'd ask Mrs Okafor in the first month instead, just to put my name down.

S4.say: I'd say farm workers need a plan this time and robot makers should pay into it. People need somewhere to go if robots come onto farms.
S4.think: Robot feeders already exist, and a farm down the road has one. If Mrs Okafor bought one plus a bedding robot, half my morning is gone, and as the junior I'm that half.
S4.do: Asks Mrs Okafor in the first month to put his name down for training on any robot feeder, rather than waiting a whole winter to see if the neighbour's works. Doubles his saving to about four hundred a month and quietly looks at work with the vet practice or the cattle market.
S4.quote: If Mrs Okafor bought one, and a robot for the bedding, half my morning is gone, and I'm the junior, so I'm the half that goes.
S4.fieldNote: His first instinct is to wait for proof, but when pushed he admits waiting is risky and would ask early. He has the sums worked out to about four months, which is why he's alarmed rather than panicked. He'd be embarrassed to move back to his mum's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help is training on the new kit paid for by whoever sells it, and maybe a rule that farms with grants for robots have to keep or retrain the staff. Something simple like that, not a big new office in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The horse owners. Everyone thinks farm money comes from food, but loads of small farms live on hay, livery and selling to hobby people. If town jobs go, we feel it even if no robot ever comes.

headlineQuote: If Mrs Okafor bought one, and a robot for the bedding, half my morning is gone, and I'm the junior, so I'm the half that goes.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old assistant stockman on a beef farm with 180 suckler cows that also sells hay to horse owners. He came from a builders' merchant three years ago, still gets nervous at calvings, and uses AI now and then to write hay adverts. He's middle-of-the-road and refuses to blame one side, but he thinks like a business owner, spotting that office layoffs would hit hay sales through horse owners. In the robot picture he knows robot feeders already exist and expects to lose half his work, and his first instinct is to wait for proof, though he admits waiting could cost him.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because robot feeders and bedding machines would take half his work and he's the junior.
whatWouldHelp: Training on new machines paid for by the sellers, and a rule that farms getting grants for robots must keep or retrain staff.
